questions.stem: A 54-year-old man presented with gradual onset epigastric pain, weight loss, and general malaise. He had moved to the UK 8 years previously. He was normally well and did not take any regular medications. He drank minimal alcohol. On examination he was afebrile and cardiovascularly stable. There was no rash or palpable lymphadenopathy. He was mildly icteric. There were several spider nevi over his torso and mild gynecomastia. Investigations: Neutrophil count 1.3 ×109/L (1.5–7.0) Platelet count 115 ×109/L (150–400) Eosinophil count 0.7 ×109/L (0.04–0.40) Serum alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (45–105) Serum alanine aminotransferase 56 U/L (5–35) Serum total bilirubin 52 μmol/L (1–22) Serum α-fetoprotein 4 kU/L (<10) Large low-attenuation mass in the liver with irregular margins; no clearly delineated walls visible. Central necrosis and irregular internal calcifications present within the lesion. Calcifications also visible on the surface of the liver.
questions.lead_in: What country carries the bulk of the global burden of this disease?
questions.explanation: China This is a case of hepatic alveolar echinococcosis, an infection with the larval stage of Echinococcus multilocularis. It can cause severe hepatic disease and, rarely, metastatic disease. E. multilocularis is restricted to the northern hemisphere. The European endemic area has expanded, but the global burden of disease lies in China. It is estimated that 91% of new cases globally each year occur in China. Cases usually become symptomatic after an incubation period of 5–15 years.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q39

b) What are 2 management options for this patient?
c) Draw the life cycle of this parasite (and indicate intermediate host(s) and definitive host(s)
d) From the cycle you draw, what are 3 possible public health interventions to decrease its incidence in countries where it is endemic?

questions.model_answer:
a) Neurocysticercosis due to the larval cyst of Taenia solium (a single enhancing parenchymal cyst); the vegetarian history fits fecal-oral acquisition of eggs from a tapeworm carrier rather than pork ingestion.
b) (1) Antiparasitic therapy for the viable parenchymal cyst — albendazole 15 mg/kg/day (max 1200 mg) divided BID for 10–14 days (add praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day if >2 cysts), with concurrent corticosteroid (dexamethasone) to blunt inflammation, and a careful eye exam beforehand to exclude ocular cysticercosis. (2) Antiseizure medication to control seizures before, during and after therapy.
c) Definitive host = humans (harbour the adult tapeworm in the intestine after eating undercooked pork containing cysticerci) and shed eggs/proglottids in feces. Intermediate host = pigs (ingest eggs → oncospheres penetrate gut → encyst as cysticerci in muscle). Humans become accidental intermediate hosts (cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis) when they ingest eggs by fecal-oral spread from a human carrier — explaining infection in a vegetarian.
d) (1) Sanitary disposal of human feces/sewage to prevent egg spread. (2) Confining/corralling pigs so they cannot access human feces, plus meat inspection and thorough cooking or freezing of pork. (3) Detection and treatment of human tapeworm carriers with health-education campaigns (with anticysticercus vaccination of pigs as an adjunct).
questions.beyond_mandell: Public-health/prevention measures are drawn from Mandell's Prevention section (p. 3472), which falls just outside the cited page range.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium). Management: Anti-seizure medication; Albendazole (15mg/kg/day divided BID for 1-2 weeks); Corticosteroids; Repeat MRI q6mos; Praziquantel (2nd line/combination for severe disease). Viable/colloidal cysts may benefit from antiparasitic medication; granular/calcified cysts do not benefit. Public health interventions: Thorough cooking of pork meat; Prompt treatment of infected people; Proper disposal of human feces; Proper hand hygiene, clean water supply; Freezing at <-10°C for >5 days. Redbook: examine stool of food handlers/child care workers recently emigrated from endemic countries; travelers should avoid uncooked unpeeled produce; screen household members for taeniasis if a member has cysticercosis.

questions.model_answer:
a) Neurocysticercosis (larval Taenia solium).
b) (1) Antiparasitic therapy for the viable parenchymal cyst — albendazole (15 mg/kg/day divided BID, +/- praziquantel if >2 cysts) for 10–14 days, preceded by an eye exam to exclude ocular cysticercosis. (2) Concurrent corticosteroid (dexamethasone 6–8 mg/day) to control treatment-induced CNS inflammation, with slow taper. (Symptomatic hydrocephalus should be shunted before antiparasitics; calcified cysts do not benefit.)
c) Humans are the definitive host, carrying the adult tapeworm after eating undercooked pork with cysticerci, and pass eggs in feces; pigs are the intermediate host, developing muscle cysticerci after ingesting eggs. Humans who swallow eggs by fecal-oral spread from a carrier become accidental intermediate hosts → cysticercosis, which is how a vegetarian is infected.
d) Careful disposal of human sewage; confining pigs and inspecting/adequately cooking or freezing pork; identifying and treating human tapeworm carriers; screening immigrants from endemic areas and household contacts; community health education.
questions.beyond_mandell: Prevention points reflect Mandell's Prevention section (p. 3472), just outside the cited range.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Neurocysticercosis. Other therapies: Albendazole +/- Praziquantel (1-2 vs >2 viable cysts), steroids prior to anti-parasitics (avoid starting anti-parasitics right away if edema/hydrocephalus, treat complications first). Lifecycle: ingestion of cysticerci by humans (undercooked pork) leads to taeniasis; embryonated eggs from soil (passed by infected human/animal) lead to oncospheres that circulate to brain (humans are definitive and dead-end host - key point despite being vegetarian, likely acquired from a Taenia solium carrier in household). Public health: handwashing, wash/peel veggies, clean water/good sanitation, screen other family members

questions.model_answer:

parts_raw.text: Name TWO species of organisms compatible with this presentation. Which is more common in Canada?
Name TWO hepatobiliary and TWO extra-hepatobiliary complications of this condition.
What are two tests that can help you diagnose and their limitations (2011)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Echinococcus granulosus (cystic/hydatid disease — the classic anechoic cyst with ‘hydatid sand’/protoscolices) and (2) Echinococcus multilocularis (alveolar disease). E. multilocularis is the species endemic across northern/Arctic Canada, so it is the more common species acquired in that region.
b) Hepatobiliary: (1) biliary obstruction/obstructive jaundice from cyst erosion into the biliary tree; (2) cholangitis or post-obstructive bacterial infection of the cyst. Extra-hepatobiliary: (1) anaphylactoid reaction on cyst rupture/leak; (2) distant daughter-cyst seeding or rupture into a bronchus/pleura (pneumothorax) with mass effect.
c) (1) Imaging (ultrasound/CT/MRI): sensitivity ≥90% and CT/MRI higher than US; limitation — appearances can mimic tumour/malignancy (especially alveolar disease). (2) Serology (ELISA/Western blot): 80–100% sensitive and 88–96% specific for liver cysts, but less sensitive for lung (50–56%) or other organs (25–56%) and cross-reacts with other cestodes; a positive scan with negative serology still supports the diagnosis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Designation of E. multilocularis as the species of northern Canada rests on Canadian/CDC-PHAC epidemiology; Mandell states only that E. multilocularis occurs in northern/Arctic North America.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort labels E. multilocularis as a ‘lung’ species and the source of the anechoic hydatid cyst; per Mandell the classic anechoic cyst with hydatid sand is E. granulosus (liver/lung), while E. multilocularis causes tumour-like liver-predominant alveolar disease.

cohort_answer.text: Species: Echinococcus granulosus (liver); Echinococcus multilocularis (lung) - most common. Complications - Hepatobiliary: Obstructive jaundice; Cholangitis. Extra-hepatobiliary: Pneumothorax; CNS involvement. Diagnostic tests: Imaging (US/CT/MRI) - could be difficult to distinguish from tumor/malignancy; Serology (IgG, Antigen) - patients with liver cysts more likely seropositive than lung cysts, 50% of patients do not have circulating antigens, less likely positive with intact/calcified/nonviable cysts; Cyst aspiration or biopsy - potential for anaphylaxis and secondary spread of infection

questions.model_answer: a) Yes. Adjunctive corticosteroids with antituberculous therapy improve neurologic outcome and mortality in tuberculous meningitis and are recommended (they are also recommended for pericardial TB). b) Yes. When cysticidal therapy (albendazole ± praziquantel) is given for viable parenchymal cysts, corticosteroids are co-administered to blunt the peri-lesional inflammatory response provoked by dying cysts. c) Yes. Corticosteroids are used in acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome) to control the systemic hypersensitivity reaction; praziquantel is added/repeated once acute illness settles. d) Yes. Peri-procedural corticosteroids are used around cyst manipulation (surgery or PAIR) to reduce the risk/consequences of anaphylaxis from spillage, alongside albendazole cover.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b–d are not covered in Mandell ch. 249; steroid use in neurocysticercosis, Katayama syndrome, and hydatid cyst manipulation reflects standard parasitology/IDSA-WHO practice.

questions.model_answer:
a) Neurocysticercosis.
b) Taenia solium (larval cyst).
c) (1) Antiparasitic therapy for viable parenchymal cysts — albendazole 15 mg/kg/day divided BID (max 1200 mg) for 10–14 days; if >2 cysts add praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day; preceded by eye exam, with corticosteroid cover; repeat course if cysts persist at 6 months. (2) Antiseizure medication before/during/after therapy, and shunting of symptomatic hydrocephalus before antiparasitics (surgery for intraventricular/ocular/spinal cysts).
d) Humans (definitive host) carry the adult tapeworm after eating undercooked pork with cysticerci and pass eggs in feces; pigs (intermediate host) develop muscle cysticerci after ingesting eggs; humans who swallow eggs by fecal-oral spread become accidental intermediate hosts → cysticercosis (explaining a vegetarian's infection).
e) Sanitary disposal of human feces; confining pigs and preventing access to human feces; meat inspection and thorough cooking/freezing of pork; detection and treatment of human tapeworm carriers; screening immigrants and household contacts; health education; anticysticercus vaccination of pigs.
questions.beyond_mandell: Prevention points reflect Mandell's Prevention section (p. 3472), just outside the cited range.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Neurocysticercosis.

B) Taenia solium.

C) Antihelminth for viable parenchymal lesions (careful eye exam preceding tx to rule out cysticercosis of the eye). Symptomatic hydrocephalus should be shunted before antihelminth tx. Contraindicated in encephalitic/disseminated neurocysticercosis, ocular disease, (untreated hydrocephalus, high cyst burden, presence of calcification). If 1-2 cysts: albendazole 15mg/kg/d div BID (max 1200mg/d) x10-14d. If >2 cysts: albendazole + praziquantel 50mg/kg/d div TID x10-14d. Retreat if parenchymal cystic lesions persist >6 months after tx. Steroid tx (adjunctive before/during antiparasitic tx) - Dex 6-8mg/day div TID x28d with slow taper over 2-8 weeks to avoid rebound. Antiseizure medication. Surgery for intraventricular/ocular/spinal cysts and those causing hydrocephalus.

D) [image-based: life cycle diagram - no text content in the slides]

E) Minimizing human consumption of contaminated pork; visible inspection of raw meat; freezing or adequately cooking meat to destroy cysticerci (pickling/salting inadequate); prevent transmission amongst pigs by eliminating access of pigs to human feces; improving sanitation for proper disposal of human waste; confine pigs so not allowed to free roam; community education re: transmission; good personal hygiene; mass community antihelminth programs to eradicate helminth carriers; vaccine (recombinant in India for pigs, not for human subjects).

questions.model_answer:
a) Echinococcus multilocularis — the Arctic/northern-Canadian Echinococcus species, causing tumour-like alveolar (multilocular) cyst disease of the liver.
b) For operable disease, wide surgical resection (e.g., hepatic lobectomy, or liver transplantation) to achieve complete removal, with adjuvant albendazole to reduce size/limit intraoperative spread. For inoperable disease, long-term (often lifelong) albendazole (or mebendazole), monitored by serial imaging and serology.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort recommends PAIR +/- albendazole; per Mandell PAIR is a treatment for cystic echinococcosis (E. granulosus, CE1/CE3a cysts), whereas alveolar disease (E. multilocularis) is managed by wide surgical resection plus prolonged albendazole, not PAIR.

cohort_answer.text:
Echinococcus multilocularis. Only echinococcus spp in Canada. Causes alveolar cyst disease
If < 5cm, medical management alone with Albendazole 10-15mg/kg/d div BID x 3-6 months. If >5cm PAIR + Albendazole x 3-6 months. PAIR: percutaneous puncture of cysts using US guidance, aspiration of cyst fluid, injection of protoscolicide for 10-15min and reaspiration of fluid. If multiple cysts: cannot do PAIR, only good for CE1 or CE3a (water lilly sign)

questions.question: A person from India is admitted with a seizure and a cyst in the brain.
questions.question_raw: Taenia solium/Neurocysticercosis: Person from India admitted with seizure and a cyst in his brain.

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
What is the likely parasitic agent?
What are two courses of management?
Draw the life cycle.

parts_raw.text: What is diagnosis?
What is likely parasitic agent?
What are 2 courses of management?
Draw the life cycle

questions.model_answer:
a) Neurocysticercosis (CNS infection with larval cysts of Taenia solium; seizures occur in up to 70% and are the most common manifestation).
b) Taenia solium (the pork tapeworm); humans acquire cysticercosis as intermediate hosts by fecal-oral ingestion of T. solium eggs.
c) Two management strategies: (1) Antiparasitic + corticosteroid therapy for viable parenchymal cysts — albendazole 15 mg/kg/day divided BID (max 1200 mg/day) for 10–14 days for 1–2 viable cysts, or albendazole plus praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day divided TID for 10–14 days for >2 cysts, with concurrent dexamethasone 6–8 mg/day for 28 days then taper; a careful eye exam must precede treatment to exclude ocular cysticercosis, and symptomatic hydrocephalus must be shunted before anthelmintics (antiparasitics are contraindicated in encephalitic/disseminated disease, ocular disease, and calcified cysts). (2) Symptomatic/surgical management — antiepileptic drugs to control seizures, and surgery (preferably endoscopic) for intraventricular cysts or shunting for hydrocephalus.
d) Life cycle: A human tapeworm carrier passes T. solium eggs in feces. Ingested eggs (fecal-oral) hatch into oncospheres in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa, enter the circulation, and encyst as cysticerci in tissues including the CNS, producing cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis. The adult tapeworm (taeniasis) is instead acquired by eating undercooked pork containing cysticerci, which mature into an intestinal adult tapeworm — completing and perpetuating the cycle.

cohort_answer.text: Neurocysticercosis. Agent: Taenia solium. Management: Antihelminth for viable parenchymal lesions (careful eye exam preceding tx to rule out ocular cysticercosis; symptomatic hydrocephalus should be shunted before antihelminth tx; contraindicated in encephalitic/disseminated neurocysticercosis, ocular disease, untreated hydrocephalus, high cyst burden, calcification); if 1-2 cysts: albendazole 15mg/kg/d div BID (max 1200mg/d) x10-14d; if >2 cysts: albendazole + praziquantel 50mg/kg/d div TID x10-14d; retreat if parenchymal cystic lesions persist >6 months after treatment; steroid tx adjunctive before/during antiparasitic tx (Dex 6-8mg/day div TID x28d with slow taper over 2-8 weeks to avoid rebound); antiseizure medication; surgery for intraventricular/ocular/spinal cysts and those causing hydrocephalus. Life cycle: cysticercosis infects humans and pigs with larval stages of Taenia solium; caused by ingestion of eggs shed in feces of human tapeworm carrier (immediately infectious, no external development needed); pigs/humans infected by ingesting eggs/gravid proglottids, usually via contaminated food/water or person-to-person spread; oncospheres hatch in intestine, invade intestinal wall, enter bloodstream, migrate to tissues/organs, mature into cysticerci over 60-70 days; some migrate to CNS causing neurocysticercosis. Differs from taeniasis (intestinal infection with adult tapeworm, acquired from undercooked pork containing cysticerci).

parts.text: Transmission of neurocysticercosis.
Diagnosis?
Treatment?
Draw the life cycle.

parts_raw.text: Transmission of neurocysticercosis
Dx?
Tx?
Draw life cycle

questions.model_answer:
a) Transmission: fecal-oral ingestion of Taenia solium eggs shed in the feces of a human tapeworm carrier (often within the same household), via contaminated food or water; the person then serves as an intermediate host and cysts develop in tissue, including the CNS.
b) Diagnosis: (1) Neuroimaging — CT/MRI showing enhancing/nonenhancing cysts, an eccentric hyperdense scolex nodule, or calcified nodules ('starry sky'); this is the most effective diagnostic modality. (2) Serology — enzyme-linked immunotransfer blot (EITB) for T. solium antibodies (sensitivity ~94% with multiple cysts, as low as 28% with single/calcified cysts). (3) CSF studies — lymphocytic/eosinophilic pleocytosis, hypoglycorrhachia, elevated protein, and lentil-lectin glycoprotein Western blot.
c) Treatment: anthelmintic plus corticosteroid for viable parenchymal cysts — albendazole 15 mg/kg/day divided BID (max 1200 mg/day) for 10–14 days for 1–2 cysts, or albendazole plus praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day divided TID for 10–14 days for >2 cysts, with dexamethasone 6–8 mg/day for 28 days then taper; precede with an eye exam to exclude ocular disease, shunt symptomatic hydrocephalus before anthelmintics, control seizures with antiepileptics, and repeat a drug course if cysts persist at 6 months. Anthelmintics are contraindicated in encephalitic/disseminated disease, ocular disease, and calcified cysts; surgery for intraventricular/spinal/ocular cysts.
d) Life cycle: eggs shed by a human T. solium tapeworm carrier are ingested (fecal-oral), hatch to oncospheres in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa, disseminate hematogenously, and encyst as cysticerci in tissue/CNS (cysticercosis). The intestinal adult tapeworm arises separately from eating undercooked pork containing cysticerci.

cohort_answer.text: Transmission: fecal-oral; ingestion of food/water contaminated with human feces, often from household tapeworm carrier shedding embryonated eggs (oncospheres) of Taenia solium. Diagnosis: Neuroimaging; Serology; PCR (CSF>Serum); Histopathology. Treatment: same as neurocysticercosis case above (antihelminth for viable parenchymal lesions with eye exam, shunt for hydrocephalus first, contraindications as above; albendazole 15mg/kg/d div BID x10-14d for 1-2 cysts, albendazole+praziquantel for >2 cysts; retreat if persist >6 months; steroid adjunctive tx; antiseizure meds; surgery for intraventricular/ocular/spinal cysts or hydrocephalus).

parts.text: Most common cause:
Two possible management strategies:
Draw the life cycle of the parasite, indicating intermediate and definitive hosts.
What public health measures can be done to reduce the transmission of this infection?

parts_raw.text: A) Most common cause:
B) 2 possible management strategies:
C) Draw the life cycle of the parasite, indicate intermediate and definitive hosts
D) What public health things can be done to reduce the transmission of this infection?

questions.model_answer:
a) Neurocysticercosis due to Taenia solium (in endemic regions, 30–50% of patients with seizures have T. solium antibodies).
b) Two strategies: (1) Anthelmintic + corticosteroid for the viable parenchymal cyst — albendazole 15 mg/kg/day divided BID (max 1200 mg/day) for 10–14 days (a single active cyst falls in the 1–2 cyst category), with dexamethasone 6–8 mg/day for 28 days then taper; precede with an eye exam, shunt hydrocephalus first if present, and retreat if the cyst persists at 6 months. (2) Symptomatic management — antiepileptic drugs to control seizures (± surgery for intraventricular/ocular/spinal cysts).
c) Life cycle: Definitive host = humans (harbor the intestinal adult tapeworm, taeniasis). Intermediate hosts = pigs (and humans, causing cysticercosis). Adult tapeworm in the human gut sheds eggs/gravid proglottids in feces; pigs (or humans) ingest eggs → oncospheres hatch, penetrate the intestinal wall, disseminate and encyst as cysticerci in muscle/tissue/CNS; humans eating undercooked cyst-infected pork acquire the adult tapeworm, completing the cycle. Human-to-human fecal-oral egg ingestion causes cysticercosis without pork.
d) Public health measures: (1) Meat control — avoid consumption of undercooked pork, inspect meat before marketing, and freeze (<−18°C) or thoroughly cook (>50°C) meat to kill cysts. (2) Sanitation — careful disposal of human sewage and preventing pig access to human feces (corralling/confining pigs). (3) Case detection and treatment — identify and treat human tapeworm carriers, including screening immigrants from endemic areas, plus health-education campaigns on self-recognition of carriers; anti-cysticercus vaccines for pigs can reduce peridomestic transmission.

cohort_answer.text: A) Neurocysticercosis. B) Antihelminth for viable parenchymal lesions (careful eye exam preceding tx; symptomatic hydrocephalus shunted before antihelminth tx; contraindicated in encephalitic/disseminated disease, ocular disease, untreated hydrocephalus, high cyst burden, calcification): if 1-2 cysts albendazole 15mg/kg/d div BID (max 1200mg/d) x10-14d; if >2 cysts albendazole + praziquantel 50mg/kg/d div TID x10-14d; retreat if lesions persist >6 months. Steroid tx (Dex 6-8mg/day div TID x28d with slow taper over 2-8 weeks); antiseizure medication; surgery for intraventricular/ocular/spinal cysts and hydrocephalus. D) Minimizing human consumption of contaminated pork; visible inspection of raw meat; freezing/adequately cooking meat (pickling/salting inadequate); prevent pig access to human feces; improve sanitation; confine pigs; community education; good hygiene; mass antihelminth programs; vaccine (recombinant, India, for pigs not humans).

questions.question: For each of the following, indicate whether you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): tuberculous meningitis; neurocysticercosis with a viable intraparenchymal cyst; cerebral malaria; acute schistosomiasis; a large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR.
questions.question_raw: For each of the following, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis; Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst; Cerebral malaria; Acute schistosomiasis; Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR.

parts.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario with rationale.

parts_raw.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario and rationale

questions.model_answer: (1) TB meningitis: YES - adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in confirmed TBM (not HIV+, where evidence is weaker). Note: steroids are NOT routine during purely empirical/diagnostic therapy as they blunt the clinical and CSF response and can worsen an undiagnosed fungal infection. (2) Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst: YES - corticosteroids control the peri-lesional inflammation/edema provoked by antiparasitic (albendazole) therapy; not indicated for calcified cysts with isolated edema. (3) Cerebral malaria: NO - randomized data show steroids are harmful (prolonged coma, more complications). (4) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama / acute neuroschistosomiasis): YES - corticosteroids given with praziquantel to suppress the hypersensitivity reaction. (5) Large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR: NO - no role for adjunctive steroids; risk is anaphylaxis, managed with antihistamines/epinephrine and peri-procedural albendazole, not steroids.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the TB-meningitis point is touched in this chapter (p. 1225, advising against routine steroids during empirical therapy). Steroid use in confirmed TBM, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, schistosomiasis, and echinococcosis/PAIR rests on IDSA/WHO guidance and the respective Mandell disease chapters, not the chronic meningitis chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Katayama fever (acute schisto) - yes (5 days pred 40mg followed by praziquantel per Mandell's). Neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes (dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days, then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels, partial reason for albendazole use in limited CNS disease). TB meningitis - yes (non-HIV TB pericarditis can also use steroids, not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence). Ruptured echinococcus - no (not addressed in guidelines or UpToDate). Cerebral malaria - no
